source_text: Παρέξομαι δὲ τῷ λόγῳ, τὴν μάλιστα ἐπιπολάζουσαν ἀνθρώποις κακοπραγίαν. Ὅταν Θεὸς μὲν τὰ καταθύμια αὐτῶν ἅπαντα ἐπιχορηγήσας. μηδένος οὐτινοσοῦν τῶν εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν ἐλθόντων αὐτὸν ἀφέληται, μὴ περιουσίας, μὴ πολυδοξίας, μὴ τῶν λοιπῶν περὶ ὅσα ἄνθρωποι ἐπτόηνται· ὁ δὲ τοῖς πᾶσιν εὐθηνούμενος, ὥσπερ τούτῳ μόνῳ θεηλάτῳ κακῷ συνεχόμενος, τῷ μὴ ἀπολαύειν, ἑταίρῳ τῷ αὐτοῦ ταμιεύσεται, πεσὼν ἄκαρπος καὶ ἑαυτῷ, καὶ τοῖς πλησίον. Τοῦτο μέγα τεκμήριον καὶ ἔλεγχον περιφανῆ ὑπερβαλλούσης ἐγὼ τίθεμαι πονηρίας· ἄνδρα τε ἐκεῖνον, ὃς πλείστων πατὴρ ὀνομασθεὶς τέκνων ἀσινῶς, βιοὺς δὲ χρόνον μακρόν, οὐκ ἐπλήσθη χρηστότητος τὴν ψυχὴν ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον, θάνατον πεῖραν οὐ λαβών· τοῦτον ἔγωγε, οὔτε τῆς πολυπαιδίας, οὔτε τῆς πολυημερίας ζηλώσαιμ᾽ ἄν· καὶ προκρίνω δὲ αὐτοῦ ἄωρον γαστρὸς μητρῴας ἐκπεσὸν ἔμβρυον. Ἐκεῖνο γὰρ ὥσπερ ἦλθε ματαίως, οὕτως ἄπεισι καὶ λαθραίως ἐν ἀμνηστίᾳ, οὐχ ἁψάμενον κακῶν, οὐδὲ προσβλέψαν ἡλίῳ. Τοῦτο κουφότερον, ἤπερ τῷ πονηρῷ, κἂν χιλίοις ἔτεσι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ζωὴν ἀναμετρησαμένῳ ἀγαθότητα μὴ ἐπιγνῷ. Τέλος δὲ ἀμφοῖν θάνατος. Ἐλεγχομένου ἄφρονος, μάλιστα τῷ πλησμονὴν μηδεμιᾶς λαμβάνειν ἐπιθυμίας. Ὁ δὲ σώφρων, τούτοις οὐκ ἐνίσχεται τοῖς πάθεσιν. Ὡς δ᾽ ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον εὐθύτης ζωῆς ἄνθρωπον τῇ πενίᾳ ὁδηγεῖ. Ἐξίστησι δὲ πολλοὺς ὀφθαλμῶν λίχνων θεάματα, τὴν ψυχὴν ἐρεθίζοντα, ἐπ᾽ ἀνόνητον σπουδὴν ἕλκοντα, διὰ τῆς τοῦ ὀφθῆναι κενῆς ἐπιθυμίας. Τὰ μέν τοι νῦν γεγεννημένα ἤδη ἔγνωσται· καὶ σαφὲς τυγχάνει, ὡς τοῖς ὑπὲρ αὐτὸν ἄνθρωπος ἀντιτάσσεσθαι οὐχ οἷός τε. Φλυαρίαι γε μὴν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους στρέφονται, τὴν τῶν χρωμένων ἄνοιαν ἐπαυξάνουσαι.
thought_title: Wealth unenjoyed and the vanity of restless desire
orientation: A man who has everything yet never enjoys it fares worse than a stillborn child, and restless desire is vanity.
pass_a_gloss: I will set forth in the discourse the ill-fortune most prevailing among men. When God, having supplied all their heart's desires, takes away from him nothing whatever of the things come into desire, not abundance, not much glory, not the rest of things over which men are excited; but he, prospering in all, as if held by this one god-driven evil, not enjoying, will store up for his companion, having fallen fruitless both to himself and to his neighbors. This I set down as a great proof and manifest refutation of surpassing wickedness; and that man who, named father of very many children unharmed, and having lived a long time, was not filled in soul with goodness for so long, not having taken experience of death: him I would not envy for many children nor for many days; and I prefer to him an untimely embryo fallen from a mother's womb. For that, as it came vainly, so departs also secretly in forgetfulness, not having touched evils, nor looked at the sun. This is lighter than for the wicked, even if, having measured out his life by a thousand years, he does not come to know goodness. End of both: death. The fool being refuted especially by taking satiety of no desire. But the prudent is not held by these passions. For the most part uprightness of life guides a man in/to poverty. Sights of greedy eyes drive many out of themselves, provoking the soul, drawing to profitless zeal, through empty desire of being seen. The things now come to be are already known; and it is clear that man is not able to set himself against those above him. Idle talks indeed turn about among men, increasing the folly of those using them.

pass_b_english: I will bring forward in my discourse the misfortune that is most widespread among human beings (Ecclesiastes 6:1). It is when God supplies everything their hearts desire and takes from a man nothing whatever of what he has longed for, neither wealth, nor great renown, nor any of the other things people are infatuated with; and yet the man who prospers in everything, as though held fast by this one evil sent by God, that he does not enjoy them, stores them up for a companion of his, and falls, bearing no fruit for himself or for his neighbors (Ecclesiastes 6:2). I count this a great sign and a plain proof of surpassing wickedness. And that man who has been called the father of a great many children without mishap, and has lived a long time, yet in all that time his soul was not filled with goodness, untouched by death: I for my part would not envy him either his many children or his many days, and I rank above him an untimely embryo fallen from its mother's womb (Ecclesiastes 6:3). For as it came in vain, so it departs unnoticed into oblivion, having touched no evils and never looked upon the sun (Ecclesiastes 6:4-5). This is lighter than the lot of the wicked man, even if he should measure out his life at a thousand years and not come to know goodness (Ecclesiastes 6:6). The end of both is death.

The fool stands exposed above all in this, that he finds no fill for any desire (Ecclesiastes 6:7); but the self-controlled man is not held fast by these passions, and as a rule uprightness of life leads a person into poverty (Ecclesiastes 6:8). Spectacles for greedy eyes drive many out of their senses: they stir up the soul and drag it toward fruitless striving through the empty desire to be seen (Ecclesiastes 6:9). What has now come to be is already known, and it is plain that a man cannot stand against those who are above him (Ecclesiastes 6:10). Idle talk, indeed, goes round among people and increases the folly of those who indulge in it (Ecclesiastes 6:11).
notes: Chapter 6 numbering is the same in English and LXX. The full stop printed after ἐπιχορηγήσας is ignored: the clause runs on into the next. 'Stores them up for a companion of his' renders ἑταίρῳ τῷ αὐτοῦ ταμιεύσεται, Gregory's form of LXX 6:2 'a stranger will eat it'; the phrase is hard and kept close. 'Untouched by death' renders θάνατον πεῖραν οὐ λαβών ('not having made trial of death'); it stands where LXX 6:3 has 'he had no burial', and may mean either that he long escaped death or that death never struck his household (compare ἀσινῶς, 'without mishap'); the English keeps both open. 'As a rule uprightness of life leads a person into poverty' renders the elliptical ὡς δ᾽ ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον εὐθύτης ζωῆς ἄνθρωπον τῇ πενίᾳ ὁδηγεῖ, following the 1622 Latin ('Fere fit autem, ut vitae rectitudo & integritas hominem ad paupertatem ducat', Opera omnia p. 87 B); the dative could instead mean 'guides a person in poverty'. It corresponds to LXX 6:8 'the poor man knows how to walk before life'. 'The fool stands exposed' renders a free-standing genitive absolute. 'To be seen' takes τοῦ ὀφθῆναι as passive (the desire for display); the 1622 Latin renders it actively ('per inanem videndi cupiditatem', 'the empty desire of seeing'). 'This is lighter than the lot of' supplies 'the lot' for ἤπερ τῷ πονηρῷ. Review check: the Opera omnia print (Paris 1622), Greek column p. 86 D (PDF leaf 110), reads ἑταίρῳ τῷ αὐτοῦ ταμιεύσεται and θάνατον πεῖραν οὐ λαβών as the copy-text does; its Latin renders them 'alii sua asservat' ('keeps his goods for another') and 'mortis interim periculo haudquaquam facto' ('never meanwhile having run the risk of death').
